## Skills

* Given a dataset, be able to determine if the appropriate assumptions are met to conduct a parametric hypothesis test 
* Identify a matched pairs design and what inference is appropriate in this situation 
* Conduct a statistical inference (confidence interval or hypothesis test) based on matched pairs data 
* Identify and justify the scope of generalizability 
* Write the parameter of interest and the hypotheses for a two-sample study 
* Interpret a p-value and evaluate the strength of evidence in a hypothesis test in the context of the study 
* Interpret a confidence interval in the context of the study 
* Evaluate a confidence interval to make a claim about the population parameter in the context of the study 
* Use the study design to determine if causality is appropriate 
* Identify and describe Type I/Type II errors in the context of the study 
* Identify and justify the study type 
* Evaluate exploratory data analysis in support of a conclusion about a parameter(s) within the context of the study 
* Justify when the results of an inference are trustworthy based on the conditions of the inferential analysis 


The above skills cover new LTs 20, 21, 22, as well as a review of LTs 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13-16, 18, and R LTs R4-R5, R10 in a new study design.

## Part 1: Bear Weights

Katmai National Park is famous for the salmon run each summer and the brown bear feast that accompanies it. Brown bears can lose roughly 30% of their body weight while hibernating (spending the winter sleeping), so it is essential that they pack on the pounds during the summer. They feed on high-caloric foods, like sockeye salmon (one salmon can be ~4000 calories), but also on sedges (a grass, often eating about 30 lbs of sedges a day), berries, grubs, etc. Over the course of the summer, bears have to add hundreds of pounds to their body weight to make up for weight lost during the past hibernation, and to survive the next hibernation; at peak season, brown bears can add up to four pounds of weight per day! Over the summer, the brown bears can really pack it on! (case in point: see pictures of the [Katmai Fat Bear champion final contenders](https://explore.org/fat-bear-week)).

You are a researcher interested in the weight gain of brown bears over the summer. You want to know if the Katmai bears, with an unusually large salmon run to feast on this year, gained more than 30% of their autumn-body weight over the summer, or roughly 345 lbs. You weigh a random selection of brown bears in Katmai NP at the beginning of June, and then weigh the same bears at the end of September and record their weight (in pounds). The data are in `fat-bear-weights.csv`, in the vectors `sept_lb` and `june_lb`.

## Section 2: Asthma & Winter Exercise 

Asthma sufferers face asthma triggers from many different fronts. Even the weather itself may pose dangers to some asthma sufferers. The cold air that winter brings has been proposed to trigger asthma attacks in asthmatic athletes. An exercise physiologist is interested in comparing peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR, L/min; a measurement of the speed of air exhaled forcefully from the lungs) in asthmatic athletes before and after they jog on a cold winter's day. *A higher PEFR indicates faster air flow from the lungs; a lower PEFR could start to indicate narrowing airways, a precursor to asthma attacks.* The exercise physiologist contacted coaches (of cardio-based sports) from their university system to recruit asthmatic athletes. Each athlete had their PEFR measured before and after a cold air jog; athletes were measured on similarly cold days and for similar jogging routes. The researchers wish to know if there is a reduction in PEFR in asthmatic athletes after they exercise in cold weather. The data are in `asthma.PEFR.csv`. Define the difference as `perf.post` - `perf.pre`. Use $\alpha - 0.05$ for the hypothesis test.
